opus-5.5.text:
I think K2 came out of a fairly simple realization: if we wanted to keep pushing the frontier, we had to go back and strengthen the base model itself. For a while, a lot of attention in the industry, including ours, was on what you can do after pretraining: reasoning, long chain-of-thought, reinforcement learning. Those things matter a lot. But at some point you see that the ceiling of everything you do afterward is set by the quality of the base model. If the foundation isn't strong enough, you're optimizing on top of a limit.

So the decision to start K2 was really about rebuilding that foundation more seriously. We asked: given the compute and data we have, how do we get the most intelligence out of each token? Token efficiency became a central question, because high-quality data isn't growing as fast as compute. That's why we spent so much effort on things like the optimizer. Muon showed it could be more token-efficient, but scaling it up exposed instability, so we had to work on making it stable at large scale. A lot of K2 was solving those very concrete engineering and research problems.

The second part was the direction of capability. We felt the next important step wasn't just a model that answers questions well, but one that can act: use tools, take multiple steps, work in an environment, and actually finish tasks. That's what we mean by agentic capability. That meant thinking from the start about what data and training would teach the model to operate, not just to chat. We put a lot of work into synthesizing agentic data and building environments for that.

And then there was the decision to open-source it. To us, that wasn't separate from the technical decision. If you believe the model is genuinely good, putting it out lets the community test it, build on it, and tell you where it falls short. It's also a way of saying that the strength of your work should be visible, not just claimed.

So overall, I see K2 less as a single product launch and more as a reset: going back to fundamentals, the base model, the training efficiency, and the agentic capability, because those are what determine how far you can go next.

r001.rationale: The response describes why K2 was started and names areas of work, such as the optimizer and agentic data, but does not frame the decision as selecting technologies to add to an already ongoing next-generation development process.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the decision to start K2 was really about returning to first principles rather than reacting to any single competitor or product cycle.

By the time we were considering it, we had spent a lot of energy on the consumer product side, and that taught us a lot about what users actually want. But it also pulled attention away from what I believe is the core question for this entire wave: how far can we push intelligence itself, and what is the most efficient path to get there? When we looked honestly at where we stood, the gap we cared about wasn't in the product layer. It was in the model layer. If the model isn't at the frontier, everything built on top of it has a ceiling, and no amount of product polish changes that.

So K2 was partly a refocusing. We decided to put the overwhelming majority of our resources into one bet: a very large model trained with a strong emphasis on token efficiency, because for us compute is the binding constraint and we can't out-spend the largest players. That forced us to think harder about optimizer design, data efficiency, and architecture choices rather than just scaling blindly. In some ways the constraint was useful. It made us ask what actually matters per unit of compute.

The other piece was agentic capability. We felt that the next meaningful step wasn't just a model that answers questions well, but one that can take actions, use tools, and carry out long multi-step tasks reliably. That requires a different kind of training emphasis from the beginning, not something you bolt on later. So K2 was designed with that direction in mind from day one.

And finally, we chose to open-source it. That was a real debate internally, but I think it reflects where we are in the ecosystem. For a team our size, openness is how you build trust, get feedback at scale, and become part of how people actually build. It also keeps us honest, because the community will test the model far more rigorously than we could alone.

So if I summarize, K2 wasn't a sudden pivot. It was us deciding to concentrate on the one thing we believe determines everything else, and to do it under our real constraints rather than pretending we had someone else's.

r001.rationale: The response describes a strategic refocusing and names model-development choices such as token efficiency, optimizer design, data efficiency, and architecture. It does not clearly frame K2 as choosing technologies to incorporate into an already ongoing next-generation model-development process.

astra-6.text:
I think of K2 as a decision about what we wanted the next stage of model development to achieve. You’re always improving the current model, but at some point you have to ask whether continuing along the same path is enough, or whether you need to pursue a more ambitious direction.

For me, the key is connecting research progress to practical capability. Can the model handle more complex tasks? Can it work through problems with less guidance? Starting K2 meant bringing those questions into a focused effort, while recognizing that we would still have to test our assumptions through the research.

r001.rationale: The response describes choosing the next stage’s goals and pursuing a more ambitious direction, but does not frame the decision as choosing which technologies to incorporate into ongoing next-generation model development.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of K2 as a decision about what we needed to learn next. When you’re developing models continuously, you can keep improving the current approach, but you also need to ask whether those improvements are taking you toward the capabilities you actually want.

So the question is: what deserves a new, focused effort? For me, that means identifying the limitations that matter most, forming a clear hypothesis about how to address them, and being willing to test it. You don’t have certainty at the beginning. The purpose of initiating a project like K2 is to turn that uncertainty into something you can investigate systematically.

r001.rationale: The response frames K2 as choosing what to learn or investigate next during ongoing model development, but does not describe choosing which technologies to incorporate into development of the next model generation.
